Hi Michael,

Thanks again for the demo last week. FinServCo is moving forward with a private deployment of Redwood in our VPC, and our security team asked for an architecture review focused on two areas: strong tenant isolation (we run multiple internal product teams in the same account) and how outbound egress from model hosts will be controlled and audited. High-level asks from security:

- A clear control-plane/data-plane demarcation and how we protect control-plane APIs (mutual TLS, IP allowlists).
- Egress channel options: per-tenant SNAT pools vs shared NAT gateway, and auditing of destination domains/IPs (we need egress logs forwarded to our SIEM).
- How KV/prefix caches and model artifacts are protected at rest and in transit.

Can we set up a short architecture review today? Ideally include someone from the infra team who owns egress policies and one of your engineers who can walk the reference diagram. I attached a list of compliance questions from our auditors (see inline).

Quick clarifications from my side before the call:
- Control plane: we recommend a customer-managed control-plane subnet with security groups limited to the customer admin IP ranges + mutual TLS between control-plane components and the private control plane agent. Control-plane endpoints can be fronted by an internal ALB with client cert validation.
- RBAC model: per-tenant service accounts + scoped API keys (no global admin key in production). We store keys in the customer KMS; Redwood only holds ephemeral certs for routing.
- Audit: our control-plane emits event logs to a configured CloudWatch/Stackdriver/SIEM endpoint via an agent; we can sign and timestamp control-plane messages if FinServCo needs non-repudiation.

Ill present the recommended control-plane config in the review and note the minimum IP ranges needed for health-checking/metrics.

Thanks for the meeting earlier — notes and a proposed dataplane change below.

Quoted text from earlier thread preserved for context.

Summary of what we walked through:
- Control plane lives in its own subnet with strict SGs; agents on host subnets authenticate via mTLS and short-lived tokens.
- For dataplane/egress we discussed three viable patterns:
  1) Shared NAT gateway (simple)
  2) Per-tenant SNAT pools (stronger isolation, separate egress IP blocks per tenant)
  3) Egress proxy chain: host -> egress-proxy in customer VPC -> corporate proxy (adds deep inspection)

My recommendation for FinServCo given audit needs: combine per-tenant SNAT pools for tenant isolation and an egress-proxy chain for deep inspection/audit. Implementation notes:
- Zone pinning: place model-host instances for sensitive tenants in dedicated AZs/subnets to limit cross-tenant blast radius.
- SNAT pools: allocate distinct Elastic IP ranges per tenant and use IPTables SNAT at the egress appliance; this simplifies firewall rules at FinServCo perimeter.
- Audit pipeline: forward egress flow logs (VPC flow logs + application-level DNS and HTTP host logs) to your SIEM via Kinesis/Logstash and retain for 13 months (complies with your policy).
- TLS termination: keep TLS end-to-end for model RPCs; TLS break only at the corporate inspection point (if required) with explicit whitelisting of Redwood package endpoints to avoid unpacked model downloads.

I attached a small example egress-policy.yaml and a zone-pinning diagram showing dedicated subnets per tenant. Also included a stubbed runbook step for how to rotate SNAT IPs without dropping active connections.

Action items we agreed:
- FinServCo to confirm required retention window for egress logs (Samantha).
- Redwood to provide terraform snippets for SNAT pool assignment and an ops runbook (Priyom to own).
- Neha to provide exact control-plane client cert requirements for procurement.

Attachments: egress-policy.yaml, zone-pinning-drawio.png

-priyom
